beginner.label: Beginner
beginner.desc: No theory background assumed: start with the feel, then see how it's used. Every term gets translated into plain language the first time it appears.

learner.label: Some Theory
learner.tagline: Turn functional harmony into a map
learner.desc: Keeps standard terms and degree logic, and adds concrete progressions, resolution directions, and paths you can actually practice.

pro.label: Musician
pro.desc: Focuses on guide tones, tension tones, voicings, substitution, and modal interchange, directly serving writing, arranging, and recording.

levelHint.beginner: Zero-background view: hear the feel first, then learn how to use it
levelHint.learner: Some-theory view: keeps degree, function, and resolution terminology
levelHint.pro: Musician view: guide tones, tension structure, and arranging detail

levelBanner.beginner: Reading in Beginner view · every explanation starts in plain language
levelBanner.learner: Reading in Some Theory view · degree and function terms are in place
levelBanner.pro: Reading in Musician view · straight to substitution, tension, and voice-leading engineering

focusLead.beginner: What it sounds like, when to use it, and where your hands go, all laid out below.
focusLead.learner: An integrated view of function, construction, voice leading, and assigned scale.
focusLead.pro: An engineering view of guide tones, tension structure, and substitute voicings.

gridHint.beginner: No need to memorize names: pick by feel first, whether stable, suspenseful, tense, or open.
gridHint.learner: Filter by category, or search chord symbols, qualities, and use cases.
gridHint.pro: Locate chord material fast by tension level and instrument suitability.

searchHint.beginner: Just type a name you know, such as maj7, sus4, or ninth chord.
searchHint.learner: Supports symbols, qualities, functions, and context keywords.
searchHint.pro: Supports term searches such as alt, upper structure, slash, and tension.

scaleLead.beginner: This group of notes is your safe zone: start by playing inside these notes.
scaleLead.learner: The natural scale of the current mode and the function of each degree.
scaleLead.pro: A comparison of modal scales, degree functions, and available tension tones.

knowledgeLead.beginner: Four of the most practical directions: grab one and start practicing.
knowledgeLead.learner: Build a framework from four dimensions: classical, jazz, modal, and arranging.
knowledgeLead.pro: Puts style grammar, modal systems, and arranging habits on the same map.

historyLead.beginner: No need to memorize dates: just see how harmony evolved step by step into what it is today.
historyLead.learner: From ancient Greece to jazz and pop, understand how functional harmony evolved.
historyLead.pro: The evolution of tuning systems, notation, and harmonic grammar, and its impact on contemporary arranging.

lead.beginner: The distance between two notes decides whether they sound close together or wide apart.
lead.learner: Degree, semitone count, and consonance are the foundation of ear training and harmonic writing.
lead.pro: Interval tendencies, resolution paths, and function within a voicing.

referenceLead.beginner: Treat this table as a distance chart: memorize the two ends first, the most stable and the most tense.
referenceLead.learner: A quick reference to how the 13 basic intervals sound and how they are commonly used.
referenceLead.pro: A complete reference of interval, tension, and resolution direction.

lead.beginner: Check whether this progression feels like setting out, leaving, and coming home.
lead.learner: Evaluate direction and cadence along the T–S–D–T function chain.
lead.pro: Four-dimension scoring: voice leading, functional strength, tension release, and stylistic fit.

emptyLane.beginner: Tap chords on the left and line them up into a harmonic route.
emptyLane.learner: Add degrees from the chord material to build an analyzable functional progression.
emptyLane.pro: Drag in degree material and see the function chain, voice smoothness, and substitution suggestions in real time.

galleryLead.beginner: Each mode is a kind of weather. Hear the brightness or darkness first, then remember one note that stands out.
galleryLead.learner: Grouped by church modes, melodic minor, pentatonic, and symmetrical scales, compare the characteristic notes.
galleryLead.pro: Search by mode family, focusing on characteristic tones, avoid notes, and chord–scale mapping.

detailLead.beginner: Hear how bright or dark it is first, then see which chords it fits.
detailLead.learner: A full view of characteristic tones, common progressions, and improv landing points.
detailLead.pro: A comparison of characteristic tones, avoid notes, upper structures, and substitute scales.

lead.beginner: Four voices are like four tracks: the goal is fewer leaps, fewer collisions, and each one moving smoothly.
lead.learner: Watch how guide tones, common tones, and parallel fifths and octaves are handled.
lead.pro: SATB voice engineering: spacing, guide-tone resolution, and hidden and parallel rules.

termsLead.beginner: When a foreign term stumps you, start with the plain-language one-liner.
termsLead.learner: A master table of terms in five languages, playing techniques, and arranging practice.
termsLead.pro: A five-language workflow reference for arranging, articulation, tempo, and form terms.

atlasLead.beginner: Learn the shape of one position first, then connect them slowly.
atlasLead.learner: A systematic atlas of CAGED, 3NP, pentatonic blues, and modern pop fingerings.
atlasLead.pro: Triple labeling of position systems, interval degrees, and actual note names.

lead.beginner: Imitate one phrase, change two notes, and eventually make it your own.
lead.learner: Filter by style, difficulty, and technique, and analyze where each phrase lands.
lead.pro: A reusable library of vocabulary, rhythmic grammar, and harmonic landing points.

lead.beginner: Wrong answers are fine: remember the sound and the shape first.
lead.learner: Drill by level and question type, and use the mistake log to find weak spots.
lead.pro: Leveled question bank and mistake review for targeted work on harmony, intervals, and terminology.

correct.beginner: Correct! Remember this feeling so it comes automatically next time.
correct.learner: Right reasoning path: identify the quality first, then rule out the distractors.
correct.pro: Correct. Worth also double-checking enharmonics, inversions, and alternate readings.

wrong.beginner: It's okay: note the correct answer first, then look back at the question.
wrong.learner: The mistake usually comes from one key condition: go back to the definition and check each item.
wrong.pro: Review: confirm whether the slip was chord quality, enharmonics, or a rule detail.

autoNext.beginner: Moving on to the next question shortly.
autoNext.learner: Moving on shortly, or tap Next question.
autoNext.pro: Auto-advances shortly, or move on manually.

lead.beginner: Fill in the skeleton first, which note on each beat, then add technique.
lead.learner: Enter by beat position and duration, and check the voices against the staff.
lead.pro: Cross-check tab against staff notation, and check technique and voice rules before exporting.

noMatch.beginner: Nothing in this part of the sky: try a simpler word.
noMatch.learner: No matches: adjust your keywords or category filters.
noMatch.pro: No matching entries: check spelling and synonyms, or clear the filters.

noData.beginner: This is still empty: add something to get started.
noData.learner: No data yet; it will show up here once you add it.
noData.pro: Empty state: no data has been created yet.

voice.beginner: How to stack the notes so it sounds good

style.beginner: Which kind of song it fits

beginner.sound: The same note, at exactly the same pitch, with no high-low difference at all.
beginner.use: Unison playing is for thickening, not octave doubling; don't mistake a perfect unison for parallel octaves.

learner.sound: Perfectly consonant, with almost no tension.
learner.use: Octave doubling can thicken the texture, but four-part writing should avoid parallel octaves.

pro.sound: Perfect unison/octave, zero beating, completely blended.
pro.use: Reinforce the root or a melodic line; watch for hidden octaves and muddiness in the low register.

beginner.sound: The two closest keys, pressed right up against each other, like a fingernail grazing a string.
beginner.use: Creates unease and suspense; it usually returns quickly to a stable note.

learner.sound: The smallest interval, strongly directional, with the highest tension.
learner.use: The core leading-tone-to-tonic resolution; can also serve as a neighbor tone or appoggiatura.

pro.sound: Minor 2nd, one of the strongest dissonances.
pro.use: A semitone resolution engine; use sparingly in the low register, often as a b9 tension.

beginner.sound: The distance of one step, like the natural lilt of speech.
beginner.use: The smoothest melodic move, used to connect two chord tones.

learner.sound: Major 2nd, a mild dissonance, the basis of stepwise motion.
learner.use: Passing and neighbor tones; harmonically it acts as a sus2 or a ninth.

pro.sound: Major 2nd, the backbone of stepwise melody.
pro.use: The source of the 9 and of sus2; mind the second clashing with the root.

beginner.sound: A little melancholy and gentle, the source of the minor sound.
beginner.use: Reach for it when you want introspection, sadness, or a night-time mood.

learner.sound: Minor 3rd, which decides the minor color.
learner.use: The third of a minor chord; with the root it creates a dark color.

pro.sound: Minor 3rd, the anchor of modal quality.
pro.use: In blues, setting it beside the major 3rd creates conflicting tension; b3 is also the source of #9.

beginner.sound: Bright and happy, the source of the major sound.
beginner.use: Use it when you want something sunny, stable, and open.

learner.use: The third of a major chord; with the root it creates a bright color.

pro.sound: Major 3rd, the core criterion of harmonic quality.
pro.use: Blues friction against b3; note that the guide tone resolves upward.

beginner.sound: Open and solemn, like an echo in a valley.
beginner.use: Creates suspense; it usually resolves back down to the third.

learner.use: The suspended fourth resolves to the third; also used in quartal stacking.

pro.use: The tension source of sus4; the basic unit of quartal voicing.

beginner.sound: The most twisted distance of all, like two forces pulling against each other.
beginner.use: The soul of the dominant chord; it badly wants to get back to something stable.

learner.sound: Augmented fourth / diminished fifth, strongly dissonant.
learner.use: The tritone of the dominant seventh, which decides the direction of resolution.

pro.sound: Tritone, the engine of dominant function.
pro.use: Tritone substitution shares the same skeleton; mind enharmonic spelling and resolution.

beginner.sound: The steadiest support, like a pillar holding up a house.
beginner.use: The skeleton of a chord; together with the root it holds the sound up.

learner.use: The chord skeleton; four-part writing avoids parallel fifths.

pro.sound: Perfect 5th, strongly related in the overtone series.
pro.use: Power chords and the bass skeleton; mind parallel and hidden fifths.

beginner.sound: A darker major sixth, like the light at dusk.
beginner.use: Adds a layer of shadow to minor or dominant chords.

learner.sound: Minor 6th, which can be seen as the inversion of an augmented fifth.
learner.use: The source of b13 color; it often resolves to the fifth or the ninth.

pro.use: The enharmonic world of b13/#5; note its substitution relationship with the fifth.

beginner.sound: Warm and flowing, like a smooth melodic line.
beginner.use: Makes a chord sound more open and more singable.

learner.use: The signature interval of sixth chords and of Dorian.

pro.use: 13 color on dominant chords; it sets a light-dark contrast with b13.

beginner.sound: A bit loose, a bit eager to move forward.
beginner.use: The key note of dominant and minor seventh chords; it pushes the music forward.

learner.sound: Minor 7th, the color of dominant and minor sevenths.
learner.use: The seventh resolving down by step is central to voice writing.

pro.sound: Minor 7th, one of the guide tones.
pro.use: Forms a tritone with the third; the resolution direction of the seventh defines harmonic grammar.

beginner.sound: A fine layer of light, gentle but a little suspended.
beginner.use: The flavor of major seventh chords; suits ballads and an urban feel.

learner.use: The hallmark of major seventh chords; usually placed in an inner voice.

pro.sound: Major 7th, a semitone clash with the root.
pro.use: The tension source of maj7; in a voicing the root or fifth can be omitted.

beginner.sound: The same note higher up, like looking in a mirror.
beginner.use: Thickens the sound, or makes a melody brighter.

learner.use: Bass thickening and unison playing; avoid parallel octaves.

pro.use: Octave stacking and arranging; mind hidden octaves and voice independence.

beginner.hint: Home. The steadiest of all; a phrase ending here feels most reassuring.

learner.hint: Tonic function, the tonal center, where cadences come to rest.

pro.hint: Tonic; can be substituted by vi/iii, but keep the root's inertia in mind.

beginner.hint: The next step. It wants to leave home a little, and often heads toward the dominant.

learner.hint: Supertonic, usually the ii pre-dominant that pushes toward V.

pro.hint: Supertonic; ii7 is the starting point of ii-V-I and can also be the tritone-sub target.

beginner.hint: The in-between color, the key note that decides major or minor.

learner.hint: Mediant, which determines major or minor quality and also substitutes for the tonic.

pro.hint: Mediant; iii7 can substitute for I; mind its guide-tone relationship to the tonic.

beginner.hint: The first step away from home, open and a little distant.

learner.hint: Subdominant, S function, often followed by V to form T-S-D-T.

pro.hint: Subdominant; IV can be borrowed as iv/IVm6, and augmented sixth chords are built from it.

beginner.hint: The note that most wants to go home: the most tension, the best payoff.

learner.hint: Dominant, D function; V7 resolving to I is the core.

pro.hint: Dominant; the V7 tritone and guide tones decide the resolution; alt and tritone sub are available.

beginner.hint: A slightly wistful substitute color, often used in place of home.

learner.hint: Submediant; vi substitutes for the tonic and often leads to IV or ii.

pro.hint: Submediant; vi7 can substitute for T and can also start a V7/ii.

beginner.hint: The note that most wants to go up, like an elevator nearing the top floor.

learner.hint: Leading tone; vii° leans strongly toward the tonic and usually carries dominant function.

pro.hint: Leading tone; vii°7 is a symmetrical diminished seventh and allows enharmonic modulation.

close.beginner: Piles all the notes together, making the chord's color easiest to hear.
close.learner: Close position: the notes sit in a narrow range, good for ear training and block chords at the keyboard.
close.pro: Close position; watch muddiness in the low register and avoid stacking below C3.

drop2.beginner: Drop the second-highest note by an octave and the sound opens up at once.
drop2.learner: Drop 2: the second-highest note moves down an octave, common in four-part writing.
drop2.pro: Drop 2; common for four-part guitar and the piano left hand; mind the spacing between voices.

drop3.beginner: Drop the third-highest note by an octave and the sound gets wider and lower.
drop3.learner: Drop 3: the third-highest note moves down an octave, giving a more open bass.
drop3.pro: Drop 3; the third-highest note drops an octave, good for mid-low positions and two-hand distribution; avoid an overly dense low register.

rootless.beginner: Skip the root and leave that space to the bass, so the color floats more.
rootless.learner: Rootless voicing, bringing out the third, seventh, and tension notes.
rootless.pro: Rootless; works with the bass; mind how 3/7 stack with the upper structure.

upper.beginner: Stack another small chord on top of a dominant chord and the color instantly sounds more sophisticated.
upper.learner: Upper structure: stacking a triad above a dominant chord to build altered tension.
upper.pro: Upper-structure triad; II/V triads over V7 are common; watch the resolution.

quartal.beginner: Stack fourths one on top of another; it sounds modern and very open.
quartal.learner: Quartal stacking breaks the tertian structure and is common in modal jazz.
quartal.pro: Quartal voicing; suits modal/So What styles; mind how it blends with the root.

chorale.beginner: Like a choir split into four voices, balanced and clean.
chorale.learner: Four-part chorale layout, handy for checking voice-leading smoothness and guide-tone resolution.
chorale.pro: SATB chorale; mind voice ranges, spacing, and parallel fifths and octaves.

guitar.beginner: On guitar, fret only the essential few notes: less effort, clearer sound.
guitar.learner: Guitar shell voicing, keeping the root, third, and seventh and omitting the fifth.
guitar.pro: Guitar shell voicing; a three/four-note skeleton; mind position and open-string resonance.

0.beginner: The classic "leave home, wander, come back" story — you hear it in almost every song.
0.learner: The T-S-D-T functional loop, a perfect cadence; the key has never been clearer.
0.pro: Authentic cadence; watch the V7 third/seventh resolution and the preparation of the cadential six-four.

1.beginner: The three building blocks jazz uses most: prepare, push, come home.
1.learner: ii7-V7-Imaj7, the core grammar of the shortest guide-tone connections.
1.pro: ii-V-I; focus on 3/7 voice leading, alt tensions, and the tritone sub.

2.beginner: The minor-key version of prepare, push, come home — darker colors, more drama.
2.learner: iiø7-V7alt-imMaj7, a strong resolution in minor.
2.pro: Minor ii-V-i; V7alt takes the altered scale, and i can be mMaj7/6/9.

3.beginner: The smoothest loop for a chorus — the emotional rise and fall lands just right.
3.learner: I-V-vi-IV: stable and singable, made for choruses.
3.pro: Pop axis; can rotate to vi-IV-I-V — mind the bass line and the hook.

4.beginner: Swap the usual dominant for a distant cousin chord, and the bass slides down by a half step.
4.learner: bII7 shares its tritone with V7, and the bass resolves down a half step.
4.pro: Tritone sub; Lydian Dominant works over bII7, where #11 is the color tone.

5.beginner: Borrow two chords from the parallel minor and the picture suddenly turns cinematic.
5.learner: Modal interchange: bVI/bVII borrowed from the parallel minor.
5.pro: Modal interchange; watch the parallel major triads of bVI-bVII-I and the voice leading.

beginner.body: Think of writing an essay: state the theme, leave it, then come home. Classical harmony is just writing that "coming home" route clearly.
points: Find the tonic first — that is home
Use IV and V to create the feeling of leaving and wanting to return
Let every voice leap as little as possible and move smoothly

learner.body: Built around key, cadence, passing harmony, and voice leading; tonic, dominant, and subdominant build a clear structure.
points: The I-IV-V-I functional loop
Resolution of neighbor tones, passing tones, and suspensions
Avoiding parallel fifths and octaves in four-part writing

pro.body: The syntax layer of functional harmony: cadences, passing six-four chords, Neapolitan and augmented sixths, pedals, and voice engineering.
points: Perfect/plagal/deceptive/imperfect cadences
Preparation and resolution of N6 and It/Fr/Ger+6
Bass line, inner voices, and harmonic rhythm

beginner.body: Jazz chords sound "thick" because sevenths and ninths sit on top of the triad. Grab the third and seventh first and you will not get lost.
points: ii-V-I is the three building blocks you will use most
The third and seventh define the chord's character
The fifth can usually be left out

learner.body: Built around functional harmony, substitute dominants, guide tones, and minimal voice movement; third and seventh first, then add tensions.
points: The core grammar of ii-V-I
Omitting the fifth keeps the voices clearer
When to use alt, sus, and upper structures

pro.body: Treat ii-V-I as a swappable syntactic unit: tritone sub, modal interchange, upper-structure triads, and chord-scale choices.
points: Guide-tone lines and 3/7 resolution
Choosing between V7alt / Lydian Dominant / Whole-tone
Drop 2/3 versus rootless — the arranging trade-off

beginner.body: A mode is the same set of notes with a different "home". Move the home and the whole color of the music changes with it.
points: First hear where the tonic is
Compare whether the third is major or minor
Remember one note that makes it distinctive

learner.body: When switching between major, minor, harmonic minor, and melodic minor, lock the tonic first, then identify the third and seventh.
points: Listen for the tonal center first
Compare major and minor thirds and sevenths
Practice parallel modes on the same tonic

pro.body: Treat modes as a chord-to-scale mapping system: characteristic notes set the color, avoid notes set the resolution, and upper structures set the voicing.
points: Quick judgment of characteristic versus avoid notes
Parallel modal interchange and borrowed chords
Voicing modal vamps and pedal points

beginner.body: The keyboard works in three layers: bass in the left hand, chords in the middle, melody in the right. On guitar, start by making sure it is playable and clear.
points: Do not let the bass get too thick
Save the melody for the right hand
Drop the fifth whenever you can

learner.body: Keyboard layers: bass and skeleton in the left hand, melody and upper structures in the right; guitar favors playable shapes and clear voices.
points: Separate bass and inner voices by register
Keep the melody and guide tones
Position beats playing every note

pro.body: Arranging is the distribution of space and function: low end for the bass, midrange for 3/7 and tensions, high end for color and melody.
points: Dividing the work between rootless voicings and the bass
Drop 2/3 and two-hand distribution
Tension density and the rhythm of resolution

historyIntro.beginner: No need to memorize dates — treat it as one storyline of music becoming freer: from single-line chant, to functional harmony, to jazz and pop.
historyIntro.learner: From Greek ratios, church modes, major/minor, and figured bass to chromaticism, the modal revival, and jazz grammar — understand the "why" of each stage.
historyIntro.pro: The coupled evolution of tuning systems, notation, and harmonic syntax: how twelve-tone equal temperament unlocked modulation, how functional harmony was dismantled by chromaticism and modal thinking, and how it reassembled in jazz and pop.
